content: Estrogen injections increase the risk of developing endometrial cancer, which is cancer of the uterine lining. The longer you use estrogen, the higher the risk. If you have not had a hysterectomy (surgical removal of the uterus), your doctor will likely prescribe a progestin to take alongside the estrogen injection. This combination may reduce the risk of endometrial cancer but could increase the risk of other conditions, such as breast cancer. Before starting estrogen injections, inform your doctor if you have or have ever had cancer or if you experience unusual vaginal bleeding. If you notice abnormal or unusual vaginal bleeding during treatment, contact your doctor immediately. Studies have shown that women who take estrogen combined with progestins orally have a higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, blood clots in the lungs or legs, breast cancer, and dementia. Women using estrogen injections, either alone or with progestins, may also face an increased risk of these conditions. Inform your doctor if you smoke or use tobacco, have had a heart attack or stroke in the past year, or if you or a family member has a history of blood clots or breast cancer. Be vigilant for symptoms that could indicate serious health issues. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of the following: sudden, severe headache or vomiting; speech difficulties; dizziness or fainting; sudden loss of vision or double vision; weakness or numbness in an arm or leg; crushing chest pain or heaviness; coughing up blood; sudden shortness of breath; difficulty thinking, remembering, or learning; breast lumps or changes; nipple discharge; or pain, tenderness, or redness in one leg. To minimize the risk of serious health problems, do not use estrogen injections, alone or with progestins, to prevent heart disease, heart attacks, strokes, or dementia. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary to manage your symptoms. Consult your doctor every 3-6 months to determine whether you should lower your dose or discontinue the medication. Perform monthly breast self-exams and have an annual mammogram and breast exam by a doctor to detect breast cancer early. Your doctor may recommend more frequent exams based on your personal or family medical history. If you are scheduled for surgery or will be on bed rest, inform your doctor. They may advise you to stop using estrogen injections 4-6 weeks beforehand to reduce the risk of blood clots. Regularly discuss the risks and benefits of estrogen injections with your doctor. Estrogen injections, specifically estradiol cypionate and estradiol valerate, are used to treat hot flashes and vaginal symptoms (dryness, itching, burning) associated with menopause. However, if you only need treatment for vaginal symptoms, alternative therapies may be more appropriate. These forms of estrogen injections are also used to treat low estrogen levels in young women who do not produce enough estrogen naturally. Estradiol valerate may also be used to alleviate symptoms of certain types of prostate cancer. Conjugated estrogen injections are used to treat abnormal vaginal bleeding caused by hormonal imbalances. Estrogen injections work by replacing the estrogen that the body normally produces. Estradiol cypionate and estradiol valerate are long-acting forms of estrogen injections administered into a muscle, typically every 3-4 weeks by a healthcare professional. When estradiol valerate is used for prostate cancer symptoms, it is usually injected every 1-2 weeks. Conjugated estrogen injections come as a powder that is mixed with sterile water and injected into a muscle or vein. This form is typically given as a single dose, with a second dose administered 6-12 hours later if needed to control vaginal bleeding. If you are using estrogen injections for hot flashes, you should notice improvement within 1-5 days. If your symptoms do not improve, inform your doctor. Before using estrogen injections, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to estrogen or any of its ingredients. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, as certain drugs may interact with estrogen. Mention any herbal products, especially St. John’s wort. Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had conditions such as yellowing of the skin or eyes during pregnancy or estrogen treatment, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, asthma, migraines, seizures, porphyria, abnormal calcium levels, or thyroid, liver, kidney, gallbladder, or pancreatic disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while using estrogen injections, contact your doctor immediately. Discuss with your doctor whether you should avoid grapefruit or grapefruit juice while using this medication. If you miss a scheduled dose, contact your doctor as soon as possible. Estrogen injections may cause side effects. Minor side effects include breast pain or tenderness, upset stomach, vomiting, weight changes, dizziness, nervousness, depression, irritability, changes in sexual desire, hair loss, unwanted hair growth, dark spots on the face, difficulty wearing contact lenses, leg cramps, and vaginal irritation or discharge. If these symptoms persist or worsen, inform your doctor. Serious side effects require immediate medical attention. These include bulging eyes, stomach pain or swelling, loss of appetite, weakness, yellowing of the skin or eyes, joint pain, uncontrollable movements, rash or blisters, hives, itching, swelling of the face or extremities, hoarseness, or difficulty breathing or swallowing. Estrogen may increase the risk of ovarian cancer or gallbladder disease requiring surgery. In children, high doses over long periods may slow growth or alter sexual development. Your child’s doctor will monitor their growth and development closely during treatment. If you experience any unusual problems or serious side effects, contact your doctor. You or your doctor may report adverse effects to the FDA’s MedWatch program. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the person is unconscious or not breathing. Symptoms of overdose include upset stomach, vomiting, and vaginal bleeding. Keep all medical appointments and inform laboratory personnel that you are using estrogen injections before undergoing any tests.
